item.title: Krill Oil
item.description:
What Is Krill Oil?

Krill oil is derived from Antarctic krill (Euphausia superba), small crustaceans approximately 1-2 cm in length that form the foundation of the Southern Ocean food chain. Krill oil is fundamentally different from conventional fish oil due to its unique lipid structure and intrinsic antioxidant content.

Biological Source:

  • Primary habitat: Antarctic waters, deepest and most pristine marine environment on Earth
  • Biomass: Estimated 500+ million tonnes; most abundant animal biomass on Earth (sustainable harvesting)
  • Natural function: Krill store lipids as energy reserves for Antarctic ecosystem, particularly for whales, penguins, and seals
  • Sustainability: Krill species are fast-reproducing, cold-water adapted; harvesting represents <1% of total biomass; certified by Marine Stewardship Council (MSC)

Unique Lipid Composition: Unlike fish oil (triglyceride-based), krill oil contains naturally occurring phospholipid-bound omega-3 fatty acids (approximately 40-50% of total lipids), which fundamentally alters bioavailability and mechanism of action.

item.title: Manganese
item.description:
What Is Manganese?

Manganese is an essential trace mineral involved in metabolic processes, bone formation, and antioxidant defense. While required in only small amounts (2-5 mg daily), manganese deficiency impairs metabolism, joint health, and oxidative stress management.

Manganese exists in oxidation states from Mn2+ to Mn7+, with Mn2+ and Mn3+ being biologically relevant. The body has limited homeostatic mechanisms for excess manganese, making toxicity possible with supplementation or environmental exposure.

item.title: Collagen
item.description:
What Is Collagen?

Collagen is the most abundant protein in the human body, comprising approximately 30% of total protein content. It’s the primary structural component of your skin, bones, tendons, ligaments, and gut lining.

Your body naturally produces collagen, but production declines with age — approximately 1% per year after age 30. Sun damage, poor nutrition, stress, and inflammation accelerate this decline. Supplemental collagen provides amino acids your body uses to rebuild and maintain collagen structures.

item.title: Curcumin
item.description:
What Is Curcumin?

Curcumin is the primary active compound in turmeric (Curcuma longa), a golden spice used for thousands of years in Ayurvedic and Traditional Chinese Medicine. It comprises only 2-8% of turmeric by weight, which is why standardized curcumin extracts are far more potent than turmeric powder alone.

Curcumin is a polyphenol—a class of plant compounds with powerful antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties. It’s one of the most researched natural compounds, with over 12,000 published studies demonstrating benefits across numerous health conditions.

item.title: Glycine
item.description:
What Is Glycine?

Glycine is the smallest and simplest amino acid, comprising approximately 35% of collagen’s amino acid composition and 10% of total body protein. Unlike the nine essential amino acids your body cannot make, glycine is a non-essential amino acid — your body produces it from serine and other amino acids.

However, endogenous production becomes insufficient under stress, intense exercise, or illness. Additionally, modern diets low in collagen-rich foods (bone broth, skin, cartilage) create relative glycine deficiency. Supplementing glycine provides building blocks for collagen, neurotransmitter synthesis, and cellular protective compounds like glutathione.
